### 294. **Run cancel still ends only the record: the session it names keeps running and spending until it ends on its own, although since WP-85 the channel that could stop it exists and the take-over already uses it** (**RESOLVED** at `ab95f9b`, WP-101, session 10 — TODO, **small — a documented limitation, not a defect**: the user guide states it (`docs/user-guide.md:397-398`, and the *not built* row at `:546`), and a human who needs the session stopped has a working command since WP-85 (take-over); **live** on every cancel of a running run, both topologies; the cost is **money**, bounded by the run's wall clock and its budget (BD-010); **read off the tree, not measured**; **unowned — for the orchestrator** (the natural owner is a successor of **WP-85**; **WP-86** is the only M5 topology row and its scope is queues and readiness); found by WP-85, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-101**, per TD-028 decision 11 (M6 amendment): option (i) — a `cancel` row when the lease is live, the record ended in place when it is not.**

**What cancel does today (refiner, read off the tree).** `cancelRunCommand` (`packages/application/src/pipeline/commands.ts:1116-1197`) wins the row through the conditional `runs.finish` with status `cancelled` and cost `null`, appends `run.finished` and pauses the task. It writes no `run_commands` row. Three consequences follow. (1) The session is never told: `run_commands.kind` admits only `'steer'` and `'take_over'` (`packages/infrastructure/src/db/migrations/0060_run_commands.sql:52`). (2) The holder's heartbeat stops at its next beat, because `renewLease` refuses a terminal row and *"the caller stops beating; it never stops the run"* (`packages/application/src/pipeline/lease.ts:147-149`, the rule at `:47-51`). So the drain WP-85 hangs on that beat stops too. (3) The `finish` that cancel wins closes every pending command of the run `run_ended` (`packages/infrastructure/src/pipeline/postgres-pipeline-store.ts:1226-1231`, `postgres-run-commands.ts:136-139`). A steer queued a moment before the cancel is therefore refused, not applied. The session then runs to its own end, its verdict is discarded (`stage-executor.ts`'s `lostTheRun`), and its spend arrives late through `runs.recordCost` (WP-47, Q70 (b)).

**The documentation half.** The route description (`apps/server/src/routes/commands.ts:984`) and the command's docblock (`packages/application/src/pipeline/commands.ts:1095-1097`) still blame this on *"Q52's out-of-process transport, which is deliberately unbuilt"*. Q52 was closed by WP-53, and WP-85 built the live-run channel. The limitation is now a choice nobody has made, not a missing transport. Q70's body says the same stale thing.

**The shape a fix would copy.** The take-over already does what cancel is missing. It pauses the task, records a `take_over` row for the live run (`commands.ts:1548-1552`), and leaves the row running. The holder calls `handle.stop` (`packages/application/src/pipeline/run-commands.ts:148-160`), and the run ends `cancelled` in its own process with its measured cost. That is Q70's closing note made true: *"with an out-of-process transport, cancel would stop the session, the spend would be known at the moment it stopped"*.

**What it costs to leave.** A cancelled run spends the rest of its session for nothing, up to its wall-clock and budget ceilings. The platform then records that spend late, and correctly. A human reading *Cancel* as *stop* pays for the difference. The user guide warns them.

**Needs a decision before starting.** When no process holds the run, or no process holds its lease (a runner down), the command must still end. Either (i) cancel records a `cancel` row and ends the record itself only when the lease is absent or expired; or (ii) it records the row *and* ends the record, and `finish`'s `run_ended` closing exempts a `cancel` row. In (ii) the holder must then stop on the notification path alone, because the heartbeat stops with the terminal row. (i) keeps one terminal writer per case; (ii) keeps today's synchronous answer.

**Done.** `run_commands.kind` admits `cancel` (a new migration; 0060 is forward-only once applied). `POST /api/runs/:run_id/cancel` records one, and the holder applies it as `handle.stop`. On WP-72's two-process topology, a cancel answered by `app` ends the session running in `runner`: the fake run stops before its script ends, the row reads `applied`, and the ledger carries the run's measured cost once. A cancel with no live holder still ends the record, as today. The route description, the docblock, the user guide at `:397-398` and `:546`, and Q70's body say which (rule 83). **Depends on** WP-85 (migration 0060). Related: **Q70**, **134**, **295**.

### 295. **The steer window is per API process, and since WP-85 every steer it admits is a paid model turn, so N processes serving the API admit N paid turns per user per five seconds** (**steer half RESOLVED** at `ab95f9b`, WP-101, session 10; the webhook-bucket half stays deferred — TODO, **small (money) — bounded, and stated at the code**: the module note says *"a deployment running N API containers allows N messages per window, which is stated here rather than discovered"* (`apps/server/src/routes/commands.ts:70-72`). Each extra turn is bounded by the run's budget (BD-010) and the task cap. **Latent with a named trigger**: more than one process serving `/api` on one database. The stock `compose.yml` runs one (`app`, `ROLE=all`, `:132`); the refiner note at `docs/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md:200` reads TD-021 as allowing API containers to be scaled. **What WP-85 changed** is the price. Before it, every steer on the shipped topology was refused `409 run_not_reachable` and refunded (backlog 134, 263), so the multiplied window admitted nothing that cost money. Now an admitted steer is recorded and applied as a user turn. **Read off the tree, not measured**; **unowned — for the orchestrator** (**WP-86** is the plausible home as M5's topology row, but none of its four criteria names the steer window); found by WP-85, session 9)
> **M7 (architect, session 11): the webhook-bucket half stays open, unscheduled — until a vendor's measured burst is reported.**
> **M6 (architect, session 9): the steer half folded into **WP-101** (shared window under a per-user advisory lock); the webhook-bucket half stays deferred until a vendor's measured burst is reported.**

> **Widened (refiner, session 9, found by WP-87): the webhook door's bucket has the same shape.** WP-87's Q60 bucket is held per process: *"The buckets are **per process**: N API replicas admit N times the policy"* (`apps/server/src/routes/webhooks.ts:40`, and technical/08:292). The policy is a constant, burst 120 at 10/s (`packages/application/src/integrations/inbound.ts:149-153`, composed at `apps/server/src/runtime.ts:964`), with no environment variable. **Graded a nit, and different from the steer half in what it costs.** A delivery past the bucket is unverified traffic, so N replicas weaken a flood shield N-fold but spend no model money. The other direction is the live one: a vendor whose legitimate burst exceeds 120 gets `429`s, and a vendor that keeps receiving errors disables its webhook (the docblock's own reason, `inbound.ts:144-146`). The operator then has no knob. The implementer, quoted: *"Not needed today; named so a later report of 429s from a real vendor has a place to land."* **Done for this half:** when such a report arrives, record the vendor's measured burst here and either make the policy configurable (an `APP_*` variable in `.env.example` and technical/12) or keep it shared with the steer window's answer (a). Until then, nothing. **Same owner as this entry (unowned).**

**What is wrong.** `createSteerGate` holds technical/08:269's *"`POST /api/runs/:id/steer` limited to 1 message per 5 s per user"* in a per-process `Map`, capped at `STEER_GATE_MAX_USERS = 4_096` with oldest-first eviction, which fails open (`apps/server/src/routes/commands.ts:221`, `:243-275`). The document states the limit per user, not per user per process. With N API processes behind a balancer, one user, or one stuck client retrying, is admitted up to N steers per window. The module note gives the limit's purpose: *"What it protects is not the platform but the **run**: each steer is a turn the model pays for"* (`:72-73`). The refiner note on Q52 (`docs/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md:200`) already filed this as backlog 38's class, and backlog 38 was resolved by WP-72 without taking it.

**What it costs to leave.** On a multi-process deployment, a run's budget is spent N times faster by repeated steers. The run cap and the task cap still stop it, so the loss is one run's budget reached sooner, never an unbounded one.

**Done.** Either (a) the window is shared state. One option is the `run_commands` rows themselves. A steer is refused when the same user has a `steer` row created within the interval. Two concurrent steers must not both pass, so this needs a per-user serialisation point. It is asserted through two `ROLE=api` processes in `test/e2e/topology/`: two steers by one user within five seconds, one per process, admit one. Or (b) the orchestrator accepts the multiplication, and technical/08:269 and the operator guide's scaling text state *per process* with the number. **Depends on** WP-85. Related: **294**, **38**, **263**.

### 296. **`APP_JOBS_SCHEMA` is read by the server and by nothing `migrate` runs, so a non-default value installs pg-boss, declares the queues and grants the app role in `pgboss` while every process looks elsewhere** (**RESOLVED** at `2177a98`, WP-106, session 11 — **ruled still latent** at WP-86's review, session 9 (the runtime's pg-boss runs `migrate: false`, so a custom schema already fails loudly at start, before and after WP-86) — TODO, **small — latent with a named trigger, and loud rather than silent on the path read off the tree**. Trigger: an operator sets `APP_JOBS_SCHEMA` to anything but `pgboss`. The stock value is `pgboss` (`.env.example:372`), which is also what `migrate` hard-wires, so a stock install is unaffected. Pre-existing; WP-86 made `migrate` the only place queues are declared ahead of a worker, so the variable now also decides where that declaration lands. **Read off the tree, not measured**; **unowned — for the orchestrator** (no M5 row names it; WP-98 is the plausible home only if the answer is option (b) below, a document-and-refusal change; option (a) is a migration and wants a row of its own); found by WP-86, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-106** — option (b): anything but `pgboss` refuses at startup, naming the variable and `migrate`.**
> **Implemented by WP-106 (session 11)**: option (b), in every server role and in `migrate`; notes under `#### WP-106`.

**What is wrong.** The variable has one reader. It is `loadJobsConfig`, `packages/infrastructure/src/jobs/config.ts:77`, and that file's own docblock at `:31` says the value *"Must match what `migrate` installed (`APP_JOBS_SCHEMA`)"*. `migrate` cannot install anything else. `apps/server/src/migrate.ts:42-48` calls `db.runMigrations` with no `pgBossSchema`, so `packages/infrastructure/src/db/migrator.ts:353` falls back to `DEFAULT_PGBOSS_SCHEMA`. The same schema then receives the WP-86 queue declaration (`:397-398`). The app role's grants are hard-wired to the literal as well: `platform_apply_grants` grants on `pgboss` only (`packages/infrastructure/src/db/migrations/0001_bootstrap.sql:295-299`). The runtime passes `config.jobs.schema` to pg-boss and to WP-86's two readers (`apps/server/src/runtime.ts:277`, `:348`, `:1046`). The operator-facing text promises a knob that does not exist: *"Change this only if migrate was run with a different schema"* (`.env.example:369-371`). `test/e2e/compose/compose-config.e2e.test.ts:538` asserts that compose delivers the variable to `migrate`, a process that never reads it.

**What happens when it is set** (read off pg-boss 12.30.0, not run). The runtime builds pg-boss with `migrate: false` (`packages/infrastructure/src/jobs/pg-boss-jobs.ts:185`). pg-boss then calls `check()` rather than installing (`node_modules/.pnpm/pg-boss@12.30.0/node_modules/pg-boss/dist/index.js:126-130`), and `check()` throws *"pg-boss is not installed"* when the schema has no version table (`dist/contractor.js:186-190`). So the likely outcome is that every process holding a job client fails at start with that message, and the operator is not told `migrate` is the cause. Once the WP-86 readers are reached they read the server's schema, so they are right exactly when the server is. **Hypothesis, the worse branch**: an operator who follows `.env.example` and installs pg-boss into the named schema by hand gets a schema with no queues declared and no grants for the app role. The likely result is permission errors, and backlog 262's `500` on `ROLE=api` back again. Needs measurement: start `app` with `APP_JOBS_SCHEMA=jobs` against a database only `migrate` touched, and record the exit and the message. The hand-installed branch needs the same measurement.

**What it costs to leave.** On a stock install, nothing. An operator who sets the variable gets an instance that does not start. The message names pg-boss, not the variable or `migrate`, and the documented remedy does not exist. It is not silent data loss, because pg-boss refuses rather than installing a second empty schema.

**Done.** Either (a) `migrate` reads the variable: `loadDatabaseConfig` or `main` passes `pgBossSchema`, and the grants take the schema as an argument, which means a new forward-only migration that replaces `platform_apply_grants`, because 0001 is applied. An integration case migrates into a non-default schema and a `ROLE=api` process enqueues into it. Or (b) the variable is removed, or refused at startup when it is not `pgboss`, and `.env.example:369-372`, `config.ts:31` and the compose-config assertion at `:538` are corrected. Either way, the process that fails names `APP_JOBS_SCHEMA` and `migrate` (rule 20). **Depends on** WP-86 (the declaration it moved into `migrate`). Related: **262**.

### 297. **technical/06 specifies a GitLab merge-request poller beside the ticket one, and WP-87 built only the ticket half: a GitLab binding with no public URL receives no `mr.*` event, so review-only mode never starts and a task never learns its merge request merged** (**RESOLVED** at `d682881`, WP-110, session 11 — TODO, **small — the design's promise is unbuilt, but every operator-facing document now says so**: the GitLab setup guide calls the webhook **required**, and the operator guide repeats it. ### 298. **A poll-only binding with a *status* pick-up rule never sees an edit once the platform's status mapping moves its ticket out of the pick-up status, so a running task keeps the ticket text it read at intake** (**RESOLVED** at `d682881`, WP-110, session 11 — TODO, **small — a stated residual that loses edits, not tickets**: WP-87 states it in the Jira setup guide and technical/06, and WP-87's criterion (2) allowed a stated *why not*. **Live** on every poll-only binding whose rule is a status (`status` rather than the default `label`). With a label rule the label stays and edits are seen. **Read off the design by the implementer, not measured**; the consumers were **read off the tree by the refiner**; **unowned — for the orchestrator** (the natural owner is a successor of WP-87, or the same row as **297**; WP-90 folds **192**, a different `ticket.updated` consumer, and does not touch the poll); found by WP-87, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-110** — each poll also reads the live tasks' tickets changed since the cursor, `ticket.updated` only.**

**What is wrong.** The poll asks only for the pick-up rule: `ticketReads(integrations).matches(plan.rule, { since, limit }, …)` (`packages/application/src/pipeline/ticket-poll.ts:306-310`). A ticket the platform moved to *In Progress* no longer matches a status rule, so no poll returns it and no `ticket.updated` is recorded. The guide states it: *"with a **status** rule, a ticket the platform has moved on to *In Progress* is no longer in the answer, and an edit to it reaches the running task only by webhook"* (`packages/integrations/src/providers/jira-cloud/setup-guide.md:120-123`). technical/06 says the same (`docs/technical/06-integrations-architecture.md:442-444`). The implementer's report names the fix: *"A second, rule-free query over the live tasks' tickets would close it at one more read per interval."*

**What the consumers of `ticket.updated` lose.** It has three consumers, and one is hit:
- **The ticket signal (WP-60), hit.** `pipeline.ticket.signal` stamps `tasks.ticket_signal_at` (`packages/application/src/pipeline/provider-signals.ts:76-94`). `isTicketSnapshotStale` re-reads only when that signal is newer than the snapshot (`ticket-snapshot.ts:490`). With no signal, no stage re-reads. The Developer, reviewer and acceptance tester are prompted with the intake-time ticket text for the rest of the task. That is backlog **187**'s edit half, narrowed from every poll-only binding to status-rule ones.
- **The *"tickets improved after lint"* metric (WP-61), not hit.** It joins `ticket.updated` to `task.lint.posted` (`apps/server/src/queries/stats-queries.ts:536-580`). The poll emits no `ticket.created`, so a poll-only binding is never linted and has nothing to improve.
- **The re-lint on edit, not built** (`provider-signals.ts:24-28`).

**What it costs to leave.** Stale requirements in the prompt when a human edits a ticket mid-task on a status-rule, poll-only binding. The agent builds to the old text, and a human finds it at review. No wrong state, no money beyond that task's rework.

**Done.** A poll also reads the tickets of the binding's **live tasks** that changed since the cursor, independent of the rule, and records each as `ticket.updated` only (never `ticket.matched`). Asserted by an integration case: a status-rule binding, a task at a later status, an edit, one poll, the signal stamped. The guide's and technical/06's residual sentences are then removed. The cost is one more read per interval, bounded by the live-task count; state that number. **Depends on** WP-87, WP-60. Related: **187**, **297**.

**Checked, not a finding** (refiner, session 9). The implementer's decision that *a binding's first poll reads its last interval only*, so an older labelled ticket (closed ones included) is not started, is **stated where an operator reads it**. The Jira setup guide says *"The first poll reads the last interval only, so a ticket labelled last month is not started by switching polling on today; touch it (any edit) and the next poll finds it"* (`packages/integrations/src/providers/jira-cloud/setup-guide.md:117-119`). technical/06 says it at `:445-447`, and `ticket-poll.ts:48-51` gives the reason. The operator guide points at that step (`docs/operator-guide.md:547-549`). The one thing the guide does not say is that a bindings `PUT` resets the cursor (stated only in migration 0061, per the WP-87 notes). That yields the same last-interval answer and starts nothing old, so it is not worth an entry.

### 299. **The Slack approval message invites *"Or reply in this thread with your reasoning."*, but a reply under a pending approval is recorded as task feedback and never reaches the approval: the platform's own message promises something the product does not do** (**RESOLVED** at `17e7318`, WP-88, session 9 (folded by the orchestrator: the approval message now says a thread reply is feedback, or the answer to the one question open there; pinned in `blocks.test.ts`) — TODO, **nit, user-visible — the fix is a one-line wording change** at `packages/integrations/src/providers/slack/blocks.ts:234`, which the orchestrator may fold into WP-88. ### 302. **The Sentry setup guide tells an operator the platform resolves the issue when the fix merges, and nothing in the build does: product/08's on-merge half of the Sentry integration is unbuilt, and three operator-facing sentences describe it as shipped** **RESOLVED** at `9a9225f`, WP-111, session 11 — (**false sentences corrected** at `6384689` by the orchestrator (the setup guide and the errors port now say resolve-on-merge is not wired); **the feature stays open** — TODO, **small — a false operator-facing sentence over an unbuilt capability**. The capability table says of `comment` *"the Sentry issue is *resolved*, which is the state change that matters"* (`:96`). §5 is headed *"Resolving on merge"* (`:102`) and tells the operator what to expect *"before you read the audit log"* (`:108`). The port's docblock says the same thing (`packages/application/src/ports/integrations/observability-errors.ts:6-7`): *"it comments on (or resolves) the issue when the fix merges"*. product/08 promises *"On merge: comment on the Sentry issue with the MR link; optional resolve-in-next-release."* (`docs/product/08-integrations.md:52`). **Nothing calls it.** `packages/application/src/pipeline/` has no caller of `resolve`, `comment` or `linkMergeRequest` on an errors port (refiner grep; the implementer's words: *"Nothing in `packages/application` calls `ObservabilityErrorsPort.resolve`, `comment` or `linkMergeRequest`"*). The adapter's `resolve` exists and is contract-tested (§5 describes its `PUT` and re-read correctly). `comment` and `linkMergeRequest` **refuse** by design (Q43's recommendation, `docs/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md:246`), so product/08's *comment* half cannot be built on documented Sentry API. **What it costs to leave.** An operator who reads the guide expects fixed issues to close themselves in Sentry. They stay open. And either (b) a merge-time `pipeline.outbound` duty on `mr.merged` for a bug task: `linkedIssues` over the ticket snapshot (WP-89's reader), `resolve(issue, {inRelease})` when a release is known, through `observabilityForProject` and the executor. Or (c) the orchestrator rules resolve-on-merge out of scope, and product/08:52 says so. **Depends on** WP-89 (`linkedIssues`, `observabilityForProject`), and on **297** for a GitLab binding without a webhook, which never sees `mr.merged`. ### 306. **The fake git provider cannot send `mr.updated.blocking_threads_resolved`, so no fake-Claude e2e drives WP-90's review-thread refresh from its `mr.updated` signal, and the one e2e that reaches its other signal asserts nothing about it** **second half RESOLVED** at `51e2440`, WP-116, session 11 — (**first half RESOLVED** at `16376e5`, WP-96, session 9 (the fake git provider can send the flag) — TODO, **small — a tier gap, not a known defect** (rule 1's shape: the fake is kinder by omission, since a signal it cannot send is a path no e2e can reach). **Live**: the refresh is shipped and asserted at the unit tier only. **Stated by the implementer, read off the tree by the refiner (grep, not run)**; **owner: WP-96** (the harness row) is the nearest, though none of its five criteria names this; found by WP-90, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): the second half folded into **WP-116**.**

**What is wrong.** The fake's merge-request delivery schema is strict and has no field for the flag: `mrEventBody` holds `event`, `project`, `iid` and an optional `updated_at` (`packages/integrations/src/git/fake.ts:373-379`), and its `mr.updated` branch builds the payload from `updated_at` alone (`:976-985`). The real half exists: the contract field is `blocking_threads_resolved: z.boolean().nullish()` (`packages/contracts/src/events.ts:674`), GitLab's normaliser sets it only when the hook's `changes` carry it (`packages/integrations/src/providers/gitlab/inbound.ts:278`), and the handler acts on `true` or `false` and ignores absence (`packages/application/src/pipeline/review-threads-refresh.ts:64-68`). The divergence register ends at 19 (`fake.ts:167`) and names no such gap. **The second signal is reachable and unasserted**: the fake can send `mr.review.comment` with `resolved` (`fake.ts:397`, `:576`), and `test/e2e/cost/human-time.e2e.test.ts:184-197` sends two resolved comments at `ready_for_merge`, the exact trigger of `review-threads-refresh.ts:70-75`. That test predates WP-90 and asserts review windows only, so since WP-90 it enqueues `review_threads_refresh` without asserting it (refiner reading; not run). Implementer's words: *"The fake git provider does not emit the flag, so no fake-Claude e2e exercises the refresh."*

**What it costs to leave.** The six unit cases in `review-threads-refresh.test.ts` drive the handler and the duty with the in-memory store. What only an e2e would catch is the full path: the normalised flag through the webhook route, the dispatcher, the `pipeline.outbound` job, the executor's `listDiscussions` read and `saveReviewThreads` against PostgreSQL, ending in the panel's count. A regression in the join (for example the duty's `mr_ref.iid` re-validation against a real task row) passes every tier.

**Done.** `mrEventBody` takes an optional `blocking_threads_resolved` boolean, the `mr.updated` branch carries it through only when present (the GitLab normaliser's absence rule), and a divergence entry says the fake sends it on request whatever the project's merge setting, which GitLab does not (GitLab sends it only on projects that require resolved threads, and only for the last resolution: WP-90 notes, `test/fixtures/http/gitlab/SOURCES.md:259`). One fake-Claude e2e: a task at `ready_for_merge` with open threads, the fake's discussions resolved, an `mr.updated` delivery with the flag, and the stored thread count reads zero open with one provider read. **Depends on** WP-90. Related: **210**, **300** (the same tier-gap shape for chat).

### 307. **WP-90's re-trace lookup runs on every `ticket.updated` of a bound project, bug or not, and no index narrows it to the ticket: its plan is either the project's whole event stream or every `ticket.bug.traced` row in the installation, across every monthly partition. Unmeasured** **RESOLVED** at `198f97b`, WP-115, session 11 — (TODO, **small — needs measurement: a hypothesis about cost, not a measured defect**. **Live**: the handler is registered on the shipped runtime. **Urgent when** a project's stream grows large, since every inbound event of a project is appended to it. **Graded by reading the query and the migrations, not by `EXPLAIN`**; **unowned — for the orchestrator** (no M5 row owns query plans; WP-97 holds technical/03 to the migrations but not to plans); found by WP-90, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-115** — measure the plan first, then bound or index.**

**What is wrong.** The query (`packages/infrastructure/src/pipeline/postgres-pipeline-store.ts:1622-1629`) filters `type = 'ticket.bug.traced'`, `stream_type = 'project' and stream_id = $1`, then two `payload` fields (the ticket's provider and key), ordered by an expression over `payload ->> 'outcome'`, then `occurred_at desc, position desc`, `limit 1`. It has **no `occurred_at` bound**. The only indexes on `events` are `(stream_type, stream_id, stream_seq)`, `(type, occurred_at)`, `correlation_id` (partial), `position` (`packages/infrastructure/src/db/migrations/0005_events.sql:31-34`) and `id` (`0010_event_dispatch.sql:29`). None is on a payload field. The table is `partition by range (occurred_at)`, monthly (`0005_events.sql:26`, `:29`). So the planner has two candidate paths, and each reads rows unrelated to the ticket: (a) the stream index reads **every event on the project's stream**, which includes every inbound event (`packages/application/src/integrations/inbound.ts:343-344` appends normalised deliveries with `stream_type: 'project'`), then filters by type and payload; or (b) the type index reads **every `ticket.bug.traced` row in the installation** (`events` has no organisation column), then filters by stream and payload. With no time bound, either path probes every partition. The `order by` expression means the `limit 1` stops nothing early; every matching row is sorted. **Two points the implementer's note does not state.** First, the handler runs for **every** `ticket.updated`, not only for bugs: it asks before it knows the ticket type, and `trace === null` is the answer for a non-bug (`packages/application/src/pipeline/delivery-measures.ts:208`, `:215`, `:220`). Second, the job asks the same query again on fire (`:394`). The docblock states it: *"measured neither way here"* (`postgres-pipeline-store.ts:1613-1617`). That is honest about the plan, but it closes by calling this *"one indexed read per ticket edit"*, and the prefix is the only part of it that is indexed.

**What it costs to leave.** A read inside the dispatcher's transaction at priority 120, on every ticket edit of every bound project. It scales with the project's history, not with the ticket. On a young install it is negligible. On a project with a year of webhook traffic, path (a) is a scan of all of it per edit, and a bulk edit multiplies that (WP-87's review round 2 treated a bulk edit of more than 50 tickets as a real case). No wrong answer, only a latency and dispatcher-hold cost that grows without bound.

**Done.** Needs measurement first (rule 27: measure before prescribing the fix). Take `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on a seeded database at two stream sizes (for example 10³ and 10⁵ project events, 10² traces), record which index is chosen and the rows read, and paste the plans here. Then either state it bounded with the numbers at the docblock, or add the narrowest fix the plan justifies: a partial expression index on `(stream_id, (payload -> 'ticket' ->> 'key'))` `where type = 'ticket.bug.traced'` (a new numbered migration, per TD-011), or a guard in the handler that skips a ticket with no prior `ticket.bug.traced` through something cheaper. Either way the docblock's *"indexed read"* clause is corrected. **Depends on** WP-90. Related: **192**.

**WP-115 measurement (session 11) — the plan, before and after migration 0071.** Machine: Apple M3 Max (14 cores, 36 GB), PostgreSQL 18 in the integration harness's Testcontainers container (`fsync=off`), warm cache, one-minute load 4–8 at every run. Seeded with set-based SQL (`generate_series`) in a throwaway integration test that is **deleted** (its seeding is kept, in the same shape, by `test/integration/db/payload-lookup-indexes.integration.test.ts`); `analyze events` after each size; each query run once to warm, then `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`. The query is the store's, byte for byte. Sizes, cumulative in one database, spread over the last 90 days (four monthly partitions populated, seven attached):

| size | the project's events | `ticket.bug.traced` in the installation | events in total |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 10³ (100 of them traces) | 1 000 (ten projects × 100) | 10 000 |
| B | 10⁵ (100 traces) | 1 100 | 110 000 |
| C | 10⁵ (the B project) | 10 100 (ninety more projects × 100) | 200 000 |

Before 0071, three plans and none of them about the ticket: A, a `BitmapAnd` of `events_*_type_occurred_at_idx` and the stream index per partition (127 buffers, 0.12–0.17 ms); B, the **installation's** traces through the type index alone, one heap page each, filtered by stream and payload afterwards (1 112 buffers, 0.36–0.45 ms); C, a `BitmapAnd` again, now over 10⁵ stream entries (1 258–1 285 buffers, 2.9–3.6 ms; the never-traced A project at C 212 buffers, 0.57 ms). A never-traced ticket (`PROJ-123`, the non-bug case) costs the same as a traced one at every size — the plan is not about the ticket. **What grows it is history, whichever of the two the planner prefers: the project's stream or the installation's traces.** Corrections to this entry, re-derived (rule 81): path (b) *is* what the planner took at B, and path (a) alone was never chosen — the costly shape at C is their intersection, which reads both. The *"one indexed read"* clause is no longer in the tree (`postgres-pipeline-store.ts`'s docblock had already been narrowed to *"not a bounded indexed read … unmeasured"*); that sentence is replaced by the measured one, and the handler's docblock (`delivery-measures.ts`) now names the non-bug case and its per-edit cost.

After 0071 (`events_bug_trace_ticket_idx (stream_id, ((payload->'ticket')->>'key')) where type = 'ticket.bug.traced'`, taken from the migration, not from a hand-made index): one index scan per partition at every size, 6–7 buffers and 0.02–0.05 ms, traced and never-traced alike. Index size 488 KiB for 10 100 traces over seven partitions; dropping and building it over size C took 38 ms. The planner's choice is held by `test/integration/db/payload-lookup-indexes.integration.test.ts` › "serves the re-trace lookup at 10^5 project events, for a traced and a never-traced ticket" (`EXPLAIN` without `ANALYZE`, the partition index names, and neither old index); canaried by changing the index predicate in the migration (fails with the message `the plan uses no partition of events_bug_trace_ticket_idx`), md5 restored.

Plans — six of the eleven taken; the five omitted (A never-traced, B traced, C never-traced, C's A project, and each of their "after") have the shape of the one shown beside them:

### 308. **First-pass acceptance matches a human comment to a task through its author's review window, not through the merge request, so a reviewer who comments on another merge request of the project during that window makes the task not first-pass: stated residual, no defect** (**CLOSED (declined for 0.1)** by the M7 architect pass, session 11; new evidence reopens it) (TODO, **nit — a stated residual, filed so it has a number**. It is stated at the predicate and in the caveat the metric publishes. **Live** on every project with reviewers who work on two merge requests at once. **Stated by the implementer, read off the tree by the refiner**; **no owner needed**; found by WP-90, session 9)
> **M9 (architect, session 12): carried, still closed — no new evidence from the first local test.**
> **M7 (architect, session 11): declined for 0.1 and closed — a stated one-way under-count, published with its caveat.**
> **M6 (architect, session 9): declined for 0.1 — a stated one-way under-count, published with its caveat.**

**What.** `HUMAN_COMMENTED` counts a `review` window when a `mr.review.comment` by the window's author, in the task's project and inside the window's span, carries no platform marker (`apps/server/src/queries/human-time-predicates.ts:73-82`). It has no merge-request term, deliberately, for `APPROVAL_TOUCHED`'s reason: a rework moves `mr_ref` (`:68-71`, and `:38-42` for the approval twin). The published caveat says it where a reader of the statistics sees it: *"A comment is matched to the task through its author's review window, not through the merge request, so a reviewer who approved this task and, inside that window, commented on another merge request of the same project makes the task not first-pass — an under-count."* (`apps/server/src/queries/stats-metrics.ts:492`). The direction is one-way (it under-counts first-pass, never over-counts). **Not pinned**: `stats-metrics.test.ts:220-229` asserts the approve-only sentence of the caveat but not this one, and the integration case covers another author and a comment outside the span, but not another merge request inside it. **Narrowing, if ever wanted:** match on the merge request each window was opened for, which needs the window row to record it. **Depends on** WP-90. Related: **191**.

### 309. **The run record does not publish `settings_hash` or the snapshot WP-91 now writes on every run, so product/09's *"exportable"* run record stores the settings it planned with and shows them to nobody** **RESOLVED** at `fde5b7f`, WP-112, session 11 — (TODO, **small — stored, not shown; no wrong value anywhere**. **Live** on every run created since WP-91. **Stated by the implementer, read off the tree by the refiner (grep, not run)**; **unowned — for the orchestrator** (WP-95 owns *"things the server publishes and no screen shows"*, and this is not yet published, so the contracts half has no row; WP-95 is the nearest carrier for the screen line); found by WP-91, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-112** — `settings_hash` on the run record and `GET /api/runs/:id/settings` at `transcript.read`.**

**What is wrong.** product/09 says the run record is *"immutable, append-only, and exportable"* (`docs/product/09-governance-cost-audit.md:37`) and lists in it *"settings snapshot (effective config hash + full copy, with secrets redacted)"* (`:39`). Since WP-91 both run-creation paths write `runs.settings_snapshot` and `runs.settings_hash` (`packages/infrastructure/src/pipeline/postgres-pipeline-store.ts:1171`, composed by `packages/application/src/pipeline/settings-snapshot.ts:80`, `:125`). Nothing reads them back: `runRecordSchema` has neither field (`packages/contracts/src/records.ts:646-670`), `GET /api/runs/:id` answers exactly that schema (`apps/server/src/routes/runs.ts:85`), and a grep for `settings_hash`/`settings_snapshot` over `apps/` outside tests finds nothing. The in-memory store says the same of its own `load` (`packages/application/src/testing/memory-pipeline.ts:795`). Implementer's words: *"It is stored, not shown: a contracts field plus a run-screen line."* The implementer also names *"the task export JSON"*; that endpoint does not exist at all, which is backlog **310**.

**What it costs to leave.** The audit question the column was written for (*"which configuration did this run plan with, and did it change between two stages?"*) is answerable only with SQL. Two runs of one task with different hashes (WP-91's criterion-1 case) look identical on the run screen.

**Done.** `runRecordSchema` gains `settings_hash: string | null` (null is *"created before WP-91"*, technical/03's stated boundary), and the snapshot is served either inline or, since it is up to 256 KiB, as its own read (for example `GET /api/runs/:id/settings`, gated like the record at `run.read`, or at `transcript.read` if the orchestrator judges operator free text in it to be content rather than metadata). It returns a typed 409 for a pre-WP-91 row, as `/prompt` does for a pre-0038 one, never `{}` served as a document. The run screen shows the hash, and marks when it differs from the task's previous run. `pnpm schemas` is regenerated, and the client census gains the call in both directions. **Depends on** WP-91. Related: **310**, **227**.

> **Left by WP-95 (session 9).** WP-95's notes list it among the items it did not take, because it needs a contracts half first: *"the run's `settings_hash` is not yet on `runRecordSchema`"*. Still unowned; **Done** above is unchanged.

### 310. **`GET /api/tasks/:id/export` is listed in technical/08, promised by product/09 and typed in contracts, and no route serves it: the task JSON export has a schema and a permission and nothing else** **RESOLVED** at `fde5b7f`, WP-112, session 11 — (TODO, **small-to-medium — a documented endpoint that does not exist**, which is the doc/code disagreement CLAUDE.md says the docs win. **Live**: the endpoint has never existed. The client census is blind to it by construction, because no screen calls it. **Found by the refiner while checking WP-91's claim that the export carries no snapshot (grep, not run)**; **unowned — for the orchestrator** (no M5 row names it); found by WP-91's report, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-112** — option (a): served at `task.export`, with an event cap.**

**What is wrong.** product/09:45 says *"Export as JSON per task."* technical/08's Tasks row lists `GET /api/tasks/:id/export` (JSON) among served endpoints with no *"not served"* qualifier (`docs/technical/08-api-and-realtime.md:17`). `taskExportResponseSchema` (`task`, `events`, `runs`, `artifacts`) is declared at `packages/contracts/src/api.ts:1536-1541`, and the permission `task.export: member` at `packages/domain/src/permissions.ts:93`, `:161`. **Nothing uses either**: a grep for `taskExportResponseSchema`/`TaskExportResponse` over `apps/` and `packages/` outside contracts finds nothing, and the server's registered `/api/tasks/:task_id…` paths are `ask`, `asks`, `audit`, `breakdown`, the eleven commands and the task read itself, with no `export`. The one earlier mention in this ledger (WP-44's decision (a), *"`task.export` is the JSON export of technical/08 and was left alone"*) read it as existing.

**What it costs to leave.** product/09's audit section ends in an export that cannot be taken, and an operator following technical/08 gets a 404. The schema also says less than product/09's task record: it has no questions, answers, returns or human actions (`:40`), and its `runs` are `runRecordSchema`, so they would carry no snapshot (**309**).

**Done.** Either (a) the route is served, gated at `task.export` and scoped to the task's project, answering one JSON document built from the existing read projections. It should include the task's audit rows and questions (product/09:40) and the run records with `settings_hash` once **309** lands. It needs a bounded-size statement (events and transcripts grow without bound, and the transcript already has its own download), a unit case through the real router with a 401/403, and a hand assertion in `client-census.test.ts` like `kb/health`'s. Or (b) the orchestrator rules it deferred, and technical/08:17 marks it *not served* with this number while product/09:45 stays a promise. **Depends on** nothing for (b); **309** for the full (a). Related: **52**.

### 311. **The pipeline's settings port and the knowledge settings read cast `projects.config` instead of parsing it, so a stored value the schema refuses reaches admission, the planner and the run's frozen snapshot, while `GET …/config` refuses the same document with a 409** (**RESOLVED** at `2177a98`, WP-106, session 11 — TODO, **small, latent — not major today, and the trigger that makes it major is named**: every API write parses, so no producer exists. **Urgent when** a release narrows the schema of any key the run path reads without a bespoke refusal like `contextBudgetRefusal`. That has happened twice already: backlog **58**, where `trigger: manual` was dropped, and WP-83's budget ceiling. SQL by an operator is the other trigger. **Read off the tree by the refiner, consequences traced by reading, not run**; **unowned — for the orchestrator** (WP-93 is the next row to write the settings port, per the plan's WP-91→WP-93 serialisation, and the nearest carrier; none of its criteria names this); found by WP-91, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): the project half folded into **WP-106** — measure the fail directions first, then parse and refuse by name at admission.**
> **Implemented by WP-106 (session 11)**: both reads parse, a failure is refused by name at admission, `contextBudgetRefusal` folded; the census is below, the notes under `#### WP-106`.

**What is wrong.** `createProjectSettingsPort` reads the row and passes `(row.config ?? {}) as ConfigValues` into the layering (`apps/server/src/pipeline.ts:700`). The knowledge read does the same (`apps/server/src/knowledge.ts:490-493`). The same function **parses** `projects.autonomy_policies` two fields later, and its comment says why (*"Parsed, not cast — … a document that does not match the current schema must not be read as one that does"*, `pipeline.ts:713-716`). `GET …/config` parses the same column with `agenticConfigSchema` and refuses `409 invalid_stored_config` (`apps/server/src/routes/projects.ts:308`). So the screen and the run disagree about one row: the screen says it is invalid, and the run proceeds on it. The residual is already stated once, at `packages/application/src/pipeline/settings.ts:146-148`, which built a refusal for the one key WP-83 narrowed instead of closing the class.

**Grade: can a refused value reach the planner?** Yes, read off the code, and `pipeline.wip` shows the direction is not uniform. `resolveWipLimits` takes `stated ?? fallback` with no check (`packages/domain/src/policies/wip.ts:56-57`), and `evaluateTaskAdmission` compares with `>=` (`:111`, `:114`). A stored `max_parallel_tasks: 0` queues every task forever under reason `wip`, with nothing naming the key (fails closed, silently). A value above the schema's 50 with no organisation bound admits that many (fails open on a limit whose purpose is spend and review load). A non-number compares `false` and admits every task (fails open). The snapshot WP-91 writes is composed from the same cast values, so it would freeze the invalid document as if it were valid. **Needs measurement:** which other keys the run path reads (commands, protected paths, reviewers, status mapping, budgets) fail open under a malformed value. That decides whether a live trigger would be major, and it is the question to answer before the fix.

**What it costs to leave.** Nothing while every row was written through the API by this release. The next schema narrowing costs either another bespoke refusal or a run planned on a value the platform's own view refuses.

**Done.** Both reads parse the settings layer with `agenticConfigSchema`. A failure **refuses the run by name** at admission, the shape `repositoryConfigRefusal` and `contextBudgetRefusal` have (key paths, redacted and bounded values, the `PUT` to make), and is never read as empty, because an empty settings layer drops restrictions somebody wrote (rule 20). `contextBudgetRefusal`'s cast-residual paragraph is then rewritten or the function folded (rule 83). There is a unit case per read with an out-of-schema `pipeline.wip` and a canary (restore the cast, and the case fails). **Depends on** nothing. Related: **58**, **173**, **224**.

> **Organisation half closed by WP-93 (session 9); the project half stays open.** The organisation document is now parsed whole at every read through `organisationSettingsFrom` (`apps/server/src/config-layers.ts:74`), called by the settings port (`apps/server/src/pipeline.ts:702`) and the organisation read (`:846`), and the per-key helpers that picked keys out of an unparsed object are gone. The project half is unchanged on the uncommitted tree. Two casts remain: `apps/server/src/pipeline.ts:705` and `apps/server/src/knowledge.ts:496`, each `(row.config ?? {}) as ConfigValues`. The WP-93 notes say plainly that it *"is not folded and stays open"*. Grade, trigger and **Done** above are unchanged.

> **Census measured by WP-106 before the fix (session 11, criterion 1).** On `6f47213`, a throw-away unit file fed each value the schema refuses into the **reader the run path calls**, through `defaultProjectSettings({ config })`, which is what the cast hands every reader. One run, deleted afterwards. *Open* means the value admits or permits more than any valid value the key could hold. *Closed* means it admits or permits less, and nothing names the key. *Throws* means a `TypeError` from inside the reader, which names no key either.
>
> | Key (reader) | Malformed stored value | Measured result | Direction |
> |---|---|---|---|

Eleven values fail open, four fail closed with no name, three throw a `TypeError` that names no key, and one, the context-budget ceiling, is refused by name. So a live trigger would be **major**: `commands.block` and the feature switches fail open on a restriction somebody wrote. The task's own cap (`taskBudgetUsd`) is not read from `projects.config` at all (the port leaves BD-010's default), so it has no row here. The run's settings snapshot freezes whatever the cast passed, so every row above is also what the run records.

> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-115**.**

The one index on the table is `(task_id, created_at desc)` (`packages/infrastructure/src/db/migrations/0004_pipeline.sql:219`), which a project-scoped export row cannot use. The export lookup is called from `GET …/config` (`apps/server/src/routes/projects.ts:501`) and from the export command (`apps/server/src/app.ts:513`). The implementer's words: *"Not measured."* **Done.** An `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` at two table sizes pasted here, then either a stated bound or a new numbered migration with a partial expression index on `(params->>'project_id', created_at desc)` (serving both reads) or a `project_id` column. **Depends on** WP-91. Related: **307** (the same unmeasured-payload-predicate shape on `events`), **52**.

**WP-115 measurement (session 11) — the plans, before and after migration 0071.** Same machine, container, load (4–8) and method as backlog 307's measurement. `human_actions` seeded set-based at **10⁴** and then to **10⁶** rows over 365 days: 95 % task commands (`params` names a task), 4 % settings writes and 1 % exports over 50 projects; the measured project has 12 rows (2 exports) at 10⁴ and 1 200 (200 exports) at 10⁶. The measured SQL was written out in drizzle's shape for the two functions; the planner test below explains the SQL captured from the real `findLastConfigExport` and `listProjectAudit` instead, so the shipped text is what is held.

Before 0071: a sequential scan of the whole table for both reads at both sizes — 167 buffers and 0.31–0.41 ms at 10⁴, **16 667–16 683 buffers and 22–27 ms** at 10⁶ (a parallel scan with two workers), the same for a project that never exported. Linear in the installation's audit, whatever the project. After 0071 (`human_actions_project_idx ((params->>'project_id'), created_at desc) where (params->>'project_id') is not null`): one index range stopped by the limit — export 62 buffers / 0.03 ms, audit 53 / 0.045 ms, a project with nothing 3 / 0.006 ms at 10⁶; at 10⁴, 14 buffers / 0.03–0.04 ms. **Its bound is the project's own settings rows**: the export read filters the action on them newest first, so a project with 1 000 settings rows and no export walks all of them (1 011 buffers, 0.2 ms, from the pre-migration probe of the same index). An expression index rather than a `project_id` column: no insert site changes, nothing to backfill, and a task command's row would hold a null there anyway. Index 3.3 MiB for 50 000 project rows; dropping and building it over 10⁶ rows took 71 ms. Held by `test/integration/db/payload-lookup-indexes.integration.test.ts` › "serves findLastConfigExport and listProjectAudit at 10^6 rows" (the SQL captured from the real functions through a drizzle logger, then `EXPLAIN`); canaried by narrowing the index predicate (fails with the message `the plan does not use human_actions_project_idx`), md5 restored.

### 313. **An open export merge request carrying an older configuration blocks a newer export until someone merges or closes it: stated residual, no defect** (**CLOSED (declined for 0.1)** by the M7 architect pass, session 11; new evidence reopens it) (TODO, **nit — decided and stated, filed so it has a number**. It is stated at the code, in the answer the operator receives and in the user guide. **Live** on every project that exports twice without merging. **Stated by the implementer, read by the refiner**; **no owner needed** unless operators find it clumsy; found by WP-91, session 9)
> **M9 (architect, session 12): carried, still closed — no new evidence from the first local test.**
> **M7 (architect, session 11): declined for 0.1 and closed — decided and stated.**
> **M6 (architect, session 9): declined for 0.1 — decided and stated; pushing onto the open export branch is a larger change nobody has asked for.**

**What.** When the previous export's merge request is `opened` or `locked`, the export answers `status: 'open'` and commits nothing (`packages/application/src/config/export.ts:295-309`), including when the open merge request carries an earlier configuration. The answer says *"no second one was opened — merge or close it, then export again"* (`:309`). The user guide says the same (`docs/user-guide.md:207`). The reason is at `:257-267`: two open merge requests writing one file conflict, and which wins is the reviewer's call. **The alternative, if ever wanted:** push the newer configuration onto the open branch, which needs the create/update judgement made against that branch rather than the default branch (the implementer's words: *"a larger change than the row"*). **Depends on** WP-91.

### 314. **Admission now takes a per-project advisory lock held to the end of the caller's transaction, so a project's intakes and scheduler passes serialise, and each waiter holds a pool connection while it waits. Unmeasured under load** **RESOLVED** at `198f97b`, WP-115, session 11 — (TODO, **small — needs measurement: a risk, not an observed defect**. The lock is correct and closes a measured race (the contract canary failed 3 of 3 without it, `expected +0 to be 1`, and passed with it). **Live** on the shipped runtime. **Urgent when** a burst of intakes arrives for one project, for example a bulk label change or a shadow batch, at a dispatcher concurrency above one. **Stated by the implementer as unmeasured, callers read by the refiner**; **unowned — for the orchestrator**; found by WP-91, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-115**.**

**What.** `tasks.counts` runs `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('task_admission/' || $1, 0))` before counting (`packages/infrastructure/src/pipeline/postgres-pipeline-store.ts:834-838`). The lock is released at commit, so it is held for the rest of the calling handler's transaction, not just the count. The callers are the intake handler (`packages/application/src/pipeline/saga.ts:534`, after the task insert, then the queue or admit writes and event appends) and `pipeline.scheduler` on `task.completed`/`cancelled`/`escalated`/`paused` (`:1592`, then a queue read and the promotions). The implementer's words: *"a project's intakes and scheduler ticks now serialise on the lock. They were already short transactions, and this was not measured under load."* **The part to measure, not asserted here:** each waiting dispatch holds a connection from the dispatcher's `2 × concurrency + 1` floor. N simultaneous intakes for one project could therefore occupy N of them while one works, delaying other projects' dispatch. **Done.** A measurement at the e2e tier: M intakes for one project delivered at once, at dispatcher concurrency above one, with an intake for a second project alongside. Record the wall time to admit all M, the second project's intake latency against the same run with the lock removed, and the pool's waiting count. Paste the numbers here, then state the bound at the port's docblock or narrow the lock's span. **Depends on** WP-91. Related: **224**, **307**.

**WP-115 measurement (session 11).** **The cause in this entry, re-derived first (rule 81), is half right.** The intake's admission does **not** run in the dispatcher: since WP-15d the intake handler only enqueues, and `tasks.counts` is called from `runIntakeCheck`'s write transaction inside a `pipeline.outbound` job (`saga.ts`, the `intake_check` duty), whose worker runs at concurrency **1 per process** (`pipeline/runtime.ts`). So one process never has two intakes waiting on each other; intakes contend only **across processes** (TD-028's topology: every `worker`/`all` process runs an outbound worker). The dispatcher half is the **scheduler** (`pipeline.scheduler`, on `task.completed`/`cancelled`/`escalated`/`paused`), which runs at up to `APP_DISPATCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY` per process and does take the lock in its dispatch. And a waiter cannot starve another project's pool: the outbound worker's one connection and each dispatch's two are already reserved in the floor (`POOL_RESERVATIONS.pipeline`, `2 × concurrency + 1`).

**Measured** at the e2e tier in a throwaway file (**deleted**): three whole `apps/server` processes on one database — one `ROLE=all`, two `ROLE=worker`, all `agent: 'none'` so nothing but admission runs — at `APP_DISPATCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY=4`, `APP_DB_POOL_MAX` = each role's floor at that concurrency + 1 (31, 29, 29), the harness's `APP_JOBS_POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS=0.5`; project B a second project of the same organisation with the same two bindings; WIP at BD-010's defaults (2 active, 5 in pipeline). **Phase 1**: M `ticket.matched` for A and one for B appended in one transaction, the B event last; sampled every 5 ms (task rows per project, each process's `pool.waitingCount`/`totalCount`, `pg_stat_activity` advisory waits). **Phase 2**: M `task.paused` for A's tasks and one for B's task, each on its own stream, so up to four scheduler dispatches per process run at once. **Lock waits of 1 ms or more are counted by the server**: `log_lock_waits = on` with `deadlock_timeout = 1ms` (`alter system`, reloaded, in the throwaway container), read off `docker logs`, and the instrument proved each run by a deliberate 30 ms advisory wait from two harness connections (logged as `acquired … after 29.6–31.6 ms` every time). *Without the lock* is the same tree with the `pg_advisory_xact_lock` statement replaced by `select $1::text` (copied, mutated, run, restored, md5 matched). Machine: Apple M3 Max, one-minute load 3.9–7.0 at the start of every run.

| lock | M | runs | phase 1: all M of A admitted | phase 1: B admitted | phase 2: all M passes | phase 2: B's pass | advisory waits ≥ 1 ms (log) | pool waiting, max per process |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| on | 20 | 9 (phase 2 in 4, log in 5) | 3 434–3 467 ms | 3 498–3 514 ms, after all of A | 79–92 ms | 79–97 ms | **0** in 5 of 5 | **0, 0, 0** in every run |
| off | 20 | 6 (phase 2 and log in 3) | 3 435–3 454 ms | 3 488–3 504 ms, after all of A | 99–156 ms | 105–162 ms | — | 0, 0, 0 |
| on | 60 | 1 | 9 998 ms | 10 288 ms | 202 ms | 208 ms | **0** | 0, 0, 0 |
| off | 60 | 1 | 10 000 ms | 10 300 ms | 266 ms | 272 ms | — | 0, 0, 0 |

No process's pool held more than 16 connections with the lock (18 without it), against a maximum of 29–31. Every phase-1 run admitted 2 of A and queued the rest; the intakes split 7/7/7 across the three processes (the fake git provider's per-process call log). **Reading it:** the lock never waited a millisecond, nobody waited for a pool connection, and B's latency is the same with and without the lock — at M = 20 and at M = 60. What sets B's latency is the outbound **queue**: B's job was enqueued after A's twenty and is taken in order, and each outbound worker takes **one job per polling interval** (21 jobs ÷ 3 workers × 0.5 s = 3.5 s, exactly the measured wall time) — pg-boss 12 re-polls immediately only for a full batch (`burstWhenBatchFull` with `batchSize > 1`, or `burstWhenReadyExceeds`), and the adapter fixes `batchSize: 1`. That is not this entry's lock and is filed as discovered work under WP-115. **Bound stated at the port** (`TaskRepository.counts`, `packages/application/src/pipeline/store.ts`) with these numbers; the lock's span is not narrowed, because nothing measured waits on it. **What the measurement did not cover**: the shipped polling default (2 s) spaces intakes further apart, so it can only lower contention; a scheduler pass that *admits* holds the lock through `step` (a few more statements), and phase 2's passes found the WIP full and returned — at M = 20 the 2 active tasks meant every pass was a count and a return.


> **Re-taken at WP-124 (session 11) at the new outbound cadence** (0.5 s for `pipeline.outbound`, 2 s for the rest): still no advisory wait of 1 ms or more and no pool waiter, at M = 20 (three runs) and M = 60 — the table is under backlog **392**.

### 315. **A project's prompt files are invisible until a run has used them: `GET …/config` publishes neither which files the last reading holds nor which a stage would be given, and a maintainer who merges an edit to `.agentic/prompts/` has no screen, API field or guide sentence saying it takes effect only at the next repository reading** **RESOLVED** at `065ae99`, WP-113, session 11 — (TODO, **small — stored, not shown; no wrong value anywhere**. Two symptoms, one cause: the reading's prompt half has no read surface. The lag itself is **working as designed** and already documented for the configuration file (technical/12:142, :270; backlog **227**, resolved by recording it rather than removing it); what is missing is that anyone can *see* it. **Live** on every project with a prompt file since WP-92. **Stated by the implementer, read off the tree by the refiner (grep, not run)**; **owner: WP-95** (the screens row) is the nearest, though its five surfaces do not include this one and the contracts half has no row; found by WP-92, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-113** — (a) to (c) of *Done*; product/13:118's diff against defaults is out of M6.**

**What is wrong.** Since WP-92 the refresh stores the `.agentic/prompts/` directory beside the configuration reading in `project_repository_config.prompts` (migration 0063, line 22; `packages/application/src/config/repository-config.ts:489`), and the settings port hands it to the planner as `repositoryPrompts` (`apps/server/src/pipeline.ts:715`). Nothing publishes it. `repositoryConfigReadingSchema` is a strict object with `path`, `status`, `commit_sha`, `read_at`, `detail` and `not_applied` and no prompts field (`packages/contracts/src/api.ts:223-231`). The settings layer's `not_applied` reports a prompt key whose value points outside the directory (`:274-279`), but not whether a correctly named file was found. product/13:118 promises that project overrides are diffed against the defaults in the UI; that is unbuilt. The implementer, quoted: *"`GET …/config` publishes neither which files the last reading holds nor which a stage would be given; product/13:118's "Project overrides are diffed against defaults in the UI" is unbuilt. The run's stored prompt shows what a run got."*

**When an edit applies.** The implementer, quoted: *"A changed prompt file applies at the next reading, like `.agentic/config.yml` (backlog 227's lag): after an index run or `POST …/config/refresh`, not at the merge."* Read off the tree: the refresh runs from the index job's `afterIndex` at the index run's commit (`apps/server/src/knowledge.ts:437-439`) and from `POST /api/projects/:project_id/config/refresh` (`apps/server/src/routes/project-config.ts:336`). The settings port reads the stored reading per stage. So a stage planned between the merge and the next index run gets the previous file's text, and a later stage of the same task can get the new one.

**What a maintainer sees today, and only after the fact.** The run record's `prompt_version` (`packages/contracts/src/records.ts:658`) moves in its `project@` lane when the delivered text changed; `GET /api/runs/:id/prompt` (`apps/server/src/routes/runs.ts:124`) shows the text the run got; `GET …/config` shows the reading's `commit_sha`/`read_at` (`apps/server/src/routes/projects.ts:442-443`), which is the commit the prompts were read at too, but nothing says prompts were part of it. A grep of `docs/user-guide.md` and `docs/operator-guide.md` for `agentic/prompts`, `prompt_append` and `config/refresh` finds nothing, so the guides do not mention the files or the lag at all.

**What it costs to leave.** A maintainer who merges a prompt edit and starts a ticket cannot tell before the run whether the edit is in effect, and a named file that is `absent`, `oversized` or `not_a_file` is reported only as a planner warning and a `status` inside a run's prompt, which is to say after a run has spent money without it.

**Done.** (a) `repositoryConfigReadingSchema` gains the prompt half of the reading: per file, the path, status (`file`/`not_a_file`/`oversized`), the pre-cut length and whether the 8 000-character cut would apply, plus `truncated`, never the text inline (it is served by the run's `/prompt` already, and a list read should stay bounded). The effective view gains, per stage, which file each of `prompt`/`prompt_append` resolves to and the status the planner would render. `pnpm schemas` is regenerated. (b) The settings screen shows both, with the reading's commit and a *Re-read now* action on the existing `POST …/config/refresh`. (c) The user guide gains a paragraph: where the files live, the two default names, the 8 000-character cut, and that an edit applies at the next index run or refresh, not at the merge. A `test:ui` case, and the client census gains nothing new unless (b) adds a call. The product/13:118 *diff against defaults* is a larger thing (it needs a notion of the shipped default per key) and should be ruled separately rather than silently folded into (b). **Depends on** WP-92. Related: **227**, **309**, **226**.

The owner line above is therefore stale: **unowned — for the orchestrator**. **Done** is unchanged.

### 316. **The stored project-prompt text is redacted by the pattern rules only, so a platform-held binding credential committed to `.agentic/prompts/` in a shape no rule knows is stored in `project_repository_config.prompts`, sent to the model verbatim, and kept in `runs.user_prompt` unless it is one of the run's own injected secrets** (**RESOLVED** at `1065d70`, WP-107, session 11 — TODO, **small — a stated residual, not a major, but wider than the residual it is compared to**. **Latent with a named trigger**: a person with merge rights commits to the default branch's `.agentic/prompts/` a credential the platform holds for a binding (a Jira, Sentry or chat token, or a GitLab token under a custom prefix, backlog **259**/**276**) that no pattern rule matches. An agent run cannot be the producer on the default path, because `.agentic/**` is in the default `protected_paths` (technical/12:113) and the file is read only from the default branch; whether a project's settings can state a `protected_paths` list without it, and so let a run propose such an edit for human merge, was **not checked**. **Graded by reading the redactor composition, not run**; **unowned — for the orchestrator** (no M5 row owns redaction at a reading); found by WP-92, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-107**, per TD-012's M6 amendment (2): option (a), the reading redacts by the project's binding credentials.**

**What is wrong.** The refresher builds `redactionAdapters.patternRedactor()` and nothing else (`apps/server/src/knowledge.ts:338-347`), and `redactedPromptReading` passes every file's text through it (`packages/application/src/config/repository-config.ts:518-529`). The comment at the refresher still says *"the only text it stores is a refusal's key paths — which a strict schema fills with typed keys"* (`knowledge.ts:338-339`), which WP-92 made untrue: it now stores up to 64 files of free text per reading. The implementer, quoted: *"The stored prompt text carries only pattern redaction (no binding's exact secret is in scope at a reading); the same residual as the configuration file's `detail`, stated rather than closed."* **The refiner's grade disagrees with "the same"**: `detail` is key paths from a strict schema, while a prompt file is arbitrary text a human wrote, so the residual is the same in kind and much wider in reach.

**Grade: can a credential the platform holds reach a prompt and a transcript this way?** Yes, on the trigger above, traced by reading. (1) At rest: the stored reading keeps it. (2) To the model: the planner renders the stored text byte-identical into a `project_prompt` block, and the runner is handed `spec.userPrompt` unredacted; the stage executor's own comment says what is stored is *"exactly the bytes the runner is handed … minus the secrets this run was given"* (`packages/application/src/pipeline/stage-executor.ts:875-889`). (3) In the transcript column: `runs.user_prompt` is redacted by `injectedSecretRedactorFor(spec)` composed with the platform redactor (`stage-executor.ts:884-889`), and the former knows only `spec.secretEnvNames` (`packages/application/src/pipeline/run-redaction.ts:46-51`, `:63-69`), i.e. the model credential and the run's git credential, not the credentials of the project's other bindings, which the loader decrypts per outbound call and never puts in a run's environment. So a Jira or Sentry token survives into `runs.user_prompt` and `GET /api/runs/:id/prompt`. The ticket path has no such gap, because the ticket snapshot is redacted with the binding's own exact-value redactor at the call. **What is not a platform defect**: a secret the project committed is already in the project's git history, and the platform cannot un-leak it. What the platform adds is two more stored copies, one readable over its API, and a copy sent to the model provider.

**What it costs to leave.** Nothing until the trigger. After it, the credential sits readable on the run's prompt read (gated at `transcript.read`) for the retention of `runs`, and the model can repeat it into an artifact. Outbound calls through `IntegrationActionExecutor` redact the *called* binding's secrets, not a different binding's.

**Done.** Either (a) the refresher composes an exact-value redactor over the decrypted credentials of the project's bindings (the loader already decrypts them; the reading runs outside any transaction, so the executor's rule is not in the way), applied to prompt texts before they are stored, with a unit case planting a non-pattern binding credential in a prompt file and asserting it is absent from the stored reading, and a canary; and the stale comment at `knowledge.ts:338-339` is rewritten. Or (b) the orchestrator rules it accepted, and the comment, the WP-92 residual and technical/05's redaction section say plainly that prompt files are pattern-redacted only and that a committed binding credential reaches the model and the run's prompt column. **Depends on** WP-92. Related: **259**, **276**, **277**.

> **Graded by WP-92's review (session 9): confirmed, minor.** The path: `refreshRepositoryConfig` redacts with `patternRedactor()` only, and the prompt write's redactor covers the run's injected environment, the credentials this process minted and the pattern rules — not a binding's static Jira, Sentry or chat token. It is **not a new trust boundary**: the same person with merge rights can already put the same token into prompts through knowledge-base documents on the default branch (the index and the context pack apply no redaction of their own), and any run with a checkout can `Read` the file. The WP-92 notes' comparison with the configuration file's `detail` residual does not hold (`detail` stores only schema key paths), and *"the run's own TD-012 redactor still covers `runs.user_prompt`"* overstates it.

### 317. **Two projects bound to one chat account with the same digest channel build the same executor idempotency key, so the second project's digest that day is answered as a replay of the first. It is never posted, and its rows are marked digested** (**RESOLVED** at `b87347a`, WP-93, session 9 (folded at review: the digest key carries the project or `org`; a two-project, one-channel case posts twice) — TODO, **major — silent loss of a human-facing message on a shipped configuration**: one Slack workspace is one account, and two projects posting to one channel is ordinary. **Latent behind a default-off switch**: it needs `features.digest.enabled` on both projects (off by default, see **301**). It fires on the first day both have something to carry. **Pre-existing since WP-32** (`675f03a`), not new with WP-93. WP-93 closed the organisation's instance of it with `:org` and found the project instance. **Stated by the implementer as read off the tree, not measured; confirmed off the uncommitted tree by the refiner (read, not run)**; **unowned — for the orchestrator**, a **one-line key change** the orchestrator may fold into WP-93; found by WP-93, session 9)

**What is wrong.** The digest's key is built from the provider, the channel and the day. It includes the project only as a null check (`packages/application/src/pipeline/integrations.ts:1913-1917`):

```ts
`${chat.ref.provider}:digest:${chat.digestChannel}:${input.day}` +
  (context.projectId === null ? ':org' : '') +
  (context.mode === 'normal' ? '' : `:${context.mode}`),
```

The executor scopes a key by `(integrationId, action, key)` (`packages/application/src/integrations/action-executor.ts:865-874`; `IdempotencyScope`, `packages/application/src/ports/integrations/audit.ts:149-153`). `integrationId` is the **account's** `integrations.id`, which every binding to that account shares (`packages/integrations/src/bindings/loader.ts:352`). `digestChannel` is per binding and falls back to the binding's `channel` when unset (`loader.ts:195-216`). So the key collides for two bindings to one account whose digest channels are equal, or whose plain channels are equal with no digest channel stated. The implementer, quoted: *"`communicationWrites.digest` keys `<provider>:digest:<channel>:<day>` and the executor scopes a key by `integrations.id` alone (`idempotencyScopeFor`), so the second project's digest that day is answered as a replay of the first's and never posted. Read off the tree, not measured."*

**Why the loss is silent (refiner, read).** `deliverDigest` makes the call (`packages/application/src/notify/digest.ts:260-262`), then marks every carried row `markDigested` (`:263-267`) and logs *"digest: posted the day’s notifications"*. A replay returns the first project's `MessageRef` as a success, so project B's rows are closed as delivered. They are never retried. No audit row reads `failed`. `digestDelivered` then skips B's day. The WP-93 comment beside the key already states the mechanism for the organisation's case (`integrations.ts:1909-1911`). Two docblocks still describe the old key shape: `digest.ts:36`, and `action-executor.ts:821`, which cites a `slack/digest.ts` plan.

**What it costs to leave.** Once two projects share a channel with digests on, every day that both have items drops one project's quiet-hours questions, approvals and reminders (the first project to run in the tick wins). The notification rows say they were delivered.

**Done.** (a) The key carries the project whenever there is one, e.g. `…:${input.day}:${context.projectId ?? 'org'}` plus the mode suffix. The project id is a platform identity, so `idempotencyScopeFor` has nothing to refuse. (b) A unit case in `notify/digest.test.ts`: two projects on one fake account and one channel, both with rows. Both digests are posted, and two distinct keys are in the store. The existing exact-key assertion at `digest.test.ts:262` is updated. A canary: with the project removed from the key, the case fails. (c) The docblocks at `digest.ts:36` and `action-executor.ts:821` are corrected. **Upgrade note:** a digest that posted under the old key on the upgrade day is not re-posted, because `digestDelivered` guards the day first. **Depends on** nothing. Related: **301**, **235**.

### 319. **A re-evaluation drafts its knowledge pages again, and a page still queued from an earlier discovery gets a second `bootstrap` proposal beside it, because the curator dedupes against the index and not against the queue** (**RESOLVED** at `bf67dd7`, WP-109, session 11 — TODO, **small — a reviewer sees one page twice and nothing links the pair**. What approving both does at the provider is **not traced**: see *needs measurement* below. **Live** since WP-94 on any project whose maintainer re-evaluates before deciding the first run's pages. That is the ordinary order: onboarding queues the pages, and a maintainer who fixed what onboarding found re-evaluates next. **Stated by the implementer, read off the uncommitted tree by the refiner (read, not run)**; **unowned — for the orchestrator** (no M5 row after WP-94 owns the proposal queue); found by WP-94, session 9)
> **M6 (architect, session 9): folded into **WP-109** — option (a): the older queued proposal for the path is discarded with a reason.**

**What is wrong.** The implementer, quoted: *"They queue as `bootstrap` proposals; the curator turns a page the index already holds into an update, but a page still queued from the first run gets a second proposal beside it (the curator dedupes against the index, not the queue)."* Read off the tree: the recorder hands `curateProposals` `indexedPaths: [...indexed.keys()]` and nothing from `kb_proposals` (`packages/application/src/onboarding/record.ts:412-420`). The curator's only cross-run dedupe is add→update for an indexed path (`packages/domain/src/knowledge/proposals.ts:306-309`). Its `claimed` set (`:236`) is per run. So each re-evaluation writes up to `MAX_DISCOVERY_DOCUMENTS` (20, `record.ts:130`) new rows under a new `task_id`, whatever is already pending for the same paths.

**What a reviewer sees (read, not run).** Two pending proposals for one `target_path`, each with its own task and delta, and no field that says one supersedes the other. The apply job takes one action per path per pass and leaves the rest for the next pass (`packages/application/src/knowledge/apply.ts:286-296`). It picks `create` or `update` from the **index** (`:313-314`), and the index holds neither page until a knowledge merge request merges. **Hypothesis, needs measurement against the fake git provider:** approving both opens two knowledge merge requests that each `create` the same file, and the second conflicts once the first merges.

**Not the retry duplicate, and its proposed fix would not catch this.** `record.ts:433-442` already states that a pg-boss retry after commit duplicates the proposals. It proposes a unique index on `kb_proposals (project_id, task_id, target_path)`. A re-evaluation is a **different task**, so that index lets this duplicate through. Whoever closes either should choose the fix with the other in view.

**What it costs to leave.** A maintainer reviews the same pages twice with nothing on the screen saying so. They can approve the older draft after the newer one. The queue grows by up to 20 rows per click, bounded by three runs per basis (`MAX_REDISCOVERY_ATTEMPTS`, `packages/application/src/onboarding/rediscovery.ts:92`).

**Done.** Either (a) the recorder reads the project's `queued` proposals and, for a path already queued, marks the older row `discarded` with a platform reason naming the newer row's task (no new status is needed: `ProposalDisposition` already has `discarded`, `proposals.ts:94-97`), or (b) it writes the new row and the queue screen groups rows by path with the newer one marked. A unit case: two discovery records for one project that draft one page leave one pending proposal under (a), or one group under (b). A canary with the read disarmed. The apply-side hypothesis above is measured or ruled out in the same change. **Depends on** WP-94. Related: **125**, **229**, **271**.

**Measured (WP-109): the apply-side hypothesis, against the fake git provider.** A throw-away contract-tier probe approved two `bootstrap` proposals for one path, from two tasks, and ran `applyKnowledgeProposals` over `createFakeGitProvider` with an empty index.
- **Confirmed: two merge requests each create the file.** The first pass took one proposal and left one (`remaining: 1`), and the second pass took the other. That gave two branches, `agentic/knowledge/2026-09-13-00000000` and `agentic/knowledge/2026-09-13-11111111`, and two merge requests, `!1` and `!2`. Each commit wrote `.agentic/knowledge/technical/overview.md` on a branch cut from a `main` without it. Each action was therefore `create`, because the fake refuses `update` on a missing path. Both rows ended `applied`.
- **Not measurable on the fake: the conflict.** That the second merge request conflicts once the first merges cannot be shown here, because the fake has no merge (its divergence 9). On a real provider it is an add/add conflict, which is **inferred**.
- **What is left after WP-109.** The undecided half of the pair no longer exists: a newer discovery draft discards an older undecided one. What remains needs an older draft that a maintainer has already **approved**. That draft is left alone by design, so the pair can still form. It is filed in WP-109's discovered work.
